  • Q: “How can I help my husband understand my ADHD so he’s not just complaining all the time about how hard this is for him?”.
  • It has been revealed that first, begin by acknowledging the truth of what he is saying: Your ADHD does, indeed, have tangible effects on him.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

“Start with an honest conversation that acknowledges the effects of your ADHD on your partner and explains how it thwarts your efforts to be the best possible spouse .”.

Q: “How can I help my husband understand my ADHD so he’s not just complaining all the time about how hard this is for him?”.

It has been revealed that first, begin by acknowledging the truth of what he is saying: Your ADHD does, indeed, have tangible effects on him. It also has emotional effects; he likely burns much more mental energy than you can see worrying about whether you completed agreed-upon tasks.

Recent findings suggest that let down your guard for an honest conversation about the impact of your actions (or inaction) on him. Show him that he matters to you and that you empathize with his experience. You may need to spend significant time here; don’t move on until you’re positive that he really feels that you get it.

[Get This Free Download: Manage ADHD’s Impact on Your Relationship].

Industry observers note that this sets the stage for the second part of the conversation — how ADHD thwarts your efforts to be the best possible partner. In other words, you have good intentions, even if they aren’t obvious, and you can feel equally frustrated and disappointed by what makes him upset. Also, your ADHD makes your life harder, not just his. While his complaints might be accurate, his too-frequent criticisms are not helping.

It has been revealed that finally, discuss how you can work together to address your hotspots. Ask: What can each of us do, or at least try to do, differently to smooth out some of our pain points? For example, do you want reminders? If so, how and when? Also, does he want to give those reminders?

It’s also helpful to discuss protocols when things don’t go according to blueprint. How and when can he bring up his concerns in a way that you can hear without getting defensive? How can you tell him that his proposed solution is not working for you?

Encourage your partner to focus on their experience rather than dissecting your actions and making declarations about why you did something.

For example, it’s more effective to say, “It stresses me out when you don’t follow through on commitments because then I feel like I have to take over, and I really don’t want to keep doing that,” versus saying, “You don’t worry about doing things because you know I’ll just do it if you don’t.”.

[Download: 5 Ways to Improve Emotional Control at Home].

I often recommend focusing your conversations on what you want in the future, not what happened in the past.

Latest Update: What is EMDR therapy, and does it actually work?

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that clinically reviewed by Dr.
  • Recent findings suggest that maybe a friend swears EMDR helped her move past something she’d carried for years.
  • If you’re uncertain, that’s understandable, because EMDR can sound unconventional: you briefly recall a painful memory while following side-to-side stimulation, like tracking a moving target with your eyes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that clinically reviewed by Dr. Chris Mosunic, PhD, RD, MBA.

Recent findings suggest that maybe a friend swears EMDR helped her move past something she’d carried for years. Or maybe you came across it online while searching for ways to cope with a memory that still feels heavy. Whether you’ve heard of EMDR but don’t know how it works, or you’re familiar with the approach but skeptical, we’re here to break it all down.

If you’re uncertain, that’s understandable, because EMDR can sound unconventional: you briefly recall a painful memory while following side-to-side stimulation, like tracking a moving target with your eyes. But the research tells a more reassuring story. It’s a well-studied therapy for trauma, and it’s increasingly explored for anxiety and depression, too.

Here’s what EMDR involves, what the research reveals, and what a session is like, so you have a clearer picture of whether it might make sense for you.

It has been revealed that EMDR stands for eye movement desensitization and reprocessing. It’s a structured therapy that helps the brain reprocess distressing memories so they carry less emotional weight. Psychologist Francine Shapiro, PhD, developed it in the late 1980s after she noticed that certain eye movements seemed to ease her own troubling thoughts.

EMDR rests on Shapiro’s adaptive information processing model. The idea is that your brain normally files an experience away, so you can recall it later without feeling like you’re living it again. But a frightening or painful event can interrupt that process, leaving the memory raw and unfiled, still carrying the fear and detail of that moment. That’s why it can resurface later, as vivid as the day it happened.

According to this model, “processing” a memory means helping your brain finish the filing. You don’t forget what happened, and the facts don’t change. What changes is the emotional charge it carries, so recalling it feels less like reliving it and more like remembering it. To help that happen, EMDR uses a technique called “bilateral stimulation.”.

According to recent reports, EMDR uses a technique called bilateral stimulation. While you hold a difficult memory in mind, a trained therapist guides you through side-to-side stimulation.

Bilateral stimulation can take a few forms:.

eye movements that follow your therapist’s fingers.

gentle taps that switch between your hands or knees.

tones that play in one ear, then the other.

According to recent reports, there’s a theory behind the side-to-side part, though researchers are still working out exactly why it helps. The leading explanation is about mental bandwidth. Your working memory, the part of your mind that holds what you’re focused on right now, can only handle so much at once. When you track side-to-side movement while recalling a hard memory, the two tasks compete for that limited space. The hard memory tends to feel a little less vivid, and with repetition it can lose its sharp edges, so it feels less overwhelming to hold.

💙 Learn more in our guide to bilateral stimulation.

Sources indicate that EMDR has eight phases, though they tend to blend together in practice. The early phases cover your history and teach you coping skills, so you feel prepared before any hard memories arise. In the middle phases, you focus on a specific memory while following bilateral stimulation, which is meant to help your brain reprocess it. The final phases check that the memory feels less distressing and help you close out the work safely.

Recent findings suggest that the evidence is strong for post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), a condition that can develop after a frightening or life-threatening event. A Cochrane review (a gold-standard summary of research on a topic) found that EMDR and trauma-focused cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) both reduce PTSD symptoms. They also outperformed other therapies when researchers checked in after treatment ended. A 2024 review in the Journal of Traumatic Stress identified more than 30 randomized controlled trials supporting EMDR for PTSD in adults and children. Major health organizations, including the World Health Organization, recommend EMDR for PTSD.

However, some guidelines, including those from the American Psychological Association (APA), rate the evidence for EMDR as less certain than for trauma-focused CBT. Researchers also debate exactly why EMDR works.

💙 Read more about how EMDR can help you cope with PTSD.

The picture is more mixed outside PTSD. Early research suggests EMDR may help with anxiety, as one meta-analysis found reduced symptoms of anxiety, panic, and phobia, though the studies were small and varied in quality.

Evidence for depression is emerging as well. Another meta-analysis highlighted reduced depression symptoms, with the strongest effects in more severe cases. These findings are promising, but they don’t carry the same weight as the PTSD research.

After you and a therapist finish the early phases, you bring a specific memory to mind and notice the thoughts and body sensations that come with it. Then your therapist guides you through the bilateral stimulation while you let your mind go where it goes. You can ask to pause or stop at any time. Unlike many talk therapies, EMDR doesn’t require you to describe the memory in detail.

Recent findings suggest that sessions usually run 60–90 minutes. Your therapist pauses often to check in on what you noticed. Over several rounds of bilateral stimulation, many people find the memory feels less sharp, even though the facts don’t change. Between sessions, a mindfulness practice, such as slow breathing or a body scan, can help you ease feelings that surface.

In a recent development, 💙 Explore Calm's EMDR-Inspired Bilateral: Anxiety, a set of music tracks that alternate gently between your left and right ear. It draws on the bilateral stimulation used in EMDR, though audio-only versions haven’t been studied on their own the way clinical EMDR has. Think of it as a calming complement to therapy, not a replacement for a trained therapist.

Sources indicate that the answer varies, since it depends on what you’re working through. For a single, recent trauma, some people notice their symptoms ease within a handful of sessions. More complex or long-standing trauma usually takes longer, sometimes many months. Therapists describe a typical course as 6–12 sessions, though it varies widely from person to person.

Along the way, some people feel worse before they feel better. Painful memories can stir up strong emotions in the short term, which is common and doesn’t mean EMDR isn’t working. Before reprocessing begins, your therapist teaches you coping skills, such as grounding exercises that anchor you in the present, so you have tools to use if those feelings get intense.

In a recent development, 💙 Try the 5, 4, 3, 2, 1 practice, a quick way to ground yourself in the present, with Prof. Megan Reitz.

EMDR stands for eye movement desensitization and reprocessing. It’s a form of therapy that uses bilateral stimulation, such as guided eye movements, to help your brain process distressing memories so they feel less intense. Psychologist Francine Shapiro developed this therapy in the late 1980s.

EMDR may help with anxiety, though PTSD is where the evidence is strongest. The studies on anxiety are smaller and less consistent. If your anxiety is tied to a specific frightening experience, it may be worth asking a therapist whether EMDR fits your situation.

💙 Explore how mindfulness can help you manage your anxiety.

EMDR differs from talk therapy because it doesn’t require you to describe your experience in detail. You’ll still talk with your therapist, especially early on, but the reprocessing happens while you hold a memory in mind and follow bilateral stimulation. Talk therapies like cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) focus more on examining and reshaping your thoughts out loud.

According to recent reports, the main benefit of EMDR is that it can ease the distress tied to painful memories. For many people with PTSD, that can mean fewer flashbacks and less of that constant, on-alert feeling.

Much of the debate is about why EMDR works, not whether it does. The evidence is strongest for PTSD, with early and more mixed findings for anxiety and depression.

According to recent reports, some studies suggest the eye movements themselves add little. The benefit may instead come from giving your mind a second task while you recall a memory, which can make it feel less vivid and emotionally intense. Other tasks that split your attention may have the same effect.

It has been revealed that certain guidelines, including the APA’s, consider the evidence for EMDR less established than for trauma-focused CBT. None of this takes away from the relief many people find with EMDR. It’s useful context as you weigh your options with a therapist.

In a recent development, EMDR is generally safe when a trained therapist delivers it, though you may experience some short-term effects. You might feel more emotional or tired between sessions, or have vivid dreams as your brain keeps processing the memory.

These reactions usually pass within a day or two. If they last longer or feel overwhelming, it’s a good idea to tell your therapist, who can adjust the pace with you. Serious side effects are uncommon when a therapist follows the full eight-phase process.

Recent findings suggest that the number of sessions you need depends on the memory you’re addressing and how long it has affected you. Some people feel relief after a few sessions, while longer-standing experiences often take more time. A common range is 6–12 sessions, but your timeline may be shorter or longer. Your therapist can give you a better sense of what to expect once they know your history.

Full EMDR needs a trained therapist, so it’s not something to try on your own. A therapist helps you reprocess memories and stay grounded if one feels overwhelming, which matters most with intense trauma.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Here are some patterns to observe to discern whether your child’s stomach pain is associated with anxiety or an underlying medical condition.

Q: “My child has anxiety and often complains of tummy aches. How do I know if the stomachaches are related to anxiety or a medical condition? How do I know when to see a doctor?”.

As parents, it’s tricky to untangle common complaints about stomachaches from chronic anxiety, an underlying medical problem, or even school avoidance. Here are a few ways to tell the difference, and clear signs that it’s time to seek medical help.

Recent findings suggest that understand the mind-body connection. Our gut and brain are in constant conversation. When a child feels overwhelmed, scared, or worried, their body will respond with stomach pain, nausea, constipation or diarrhea, and a generalized discomfort. These symptoms are not imagined or exaggerated; they are physical reactions to emotional stress.

[Download: 5 Ways to Improve Emotional Control at Home].

Observe timing and patterns. When are stomachaches happening? Stomach pain related to anxiety trends to show up during specific times: before and around school, tests, social events, and bedtime. Does your child’s stomachache dissipate after these types of events, or when they are comforted or distracted?

Are your child’s stomach pains taking place at night? Are they making it difficult for your child to eat? Are they losing weight? Is your child experiencing chronic diarrhea or do they have blood in their stool? Are they vomiting? These symptoms are more indicative of an underlying medical condition, especially if they become worse over time.

Keep a log. Track when your child has stomach pains to help you discern whether it’s due to anxiety or an underlying medical condition. Occasional stomachaches that happen during stressful times are common.

However, if your child complains of a stomachache several times each week for more than a month, consult with your pediatrician or seek a gastroenterologist.

[Read: “5 Ways to Reframe Anxiety for Your Worried Teen”].

Recent findings suggest that and remember: You don’t have to choose between taking anxiety seriously and taking physical symptoms seriously. Both deserve attention. By watching for patterns, listening carefully, and seeking help when needed, you’re doing exactly what your child needs: letting them know that any pain they experience matters.

Liz Nissim, Ph.D., is a clinical and school psychologist specializing in parenting and executive function coaching for neurodivergent children and teens.

#10605. Breaking: Can you be friends with your ex? What to consider first

📅 09 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1446 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Calm ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: Can you be friends with your ex? What to consider first

📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1446 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Calm

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that your phone buzzes.
  • Moments like this are why staying friends with an ex can feel so confusing.
  • Whether you’re the one hoping to stay in touch or the one being asked to, here’s how to tell if staying friends would help you move on or make it harder.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that your phone buzzes. It’s your ex, sending a meme you would’ve laughed at together six months ago. You smile, then wonder why you smiled.

Moments like this are why staying friends with an ex can feel so confusing. For some people, staying connected feels natural because the habit, and maybe the care, is still there. For others, it makes healing feel harder. Every situation is different, and you’re allowed to take your time figuring out what works for you.

Whether you’re the one hoping to stay in touch or the one being asked to, here’s how to tell if staying friends would help you move on or make it harder.

In some cases, you may be able to. Post-breakup friendships can be healthy and meaningful when the breakup was mutual, the relationship had little conflict, and both people have had time to grieve.

That said, every friendship between exes is different. Researchers who study friendships after breakups describe two kinds. In one, both people have moved on and value the connection. In the other, one or both people stay in touch because of lingering attraction or reluctance to end things. The first kind can be rewarding. The second can make it harder to get over the breakup.

The dynamic you had with your ex matters, too. A study found that relationships shaped by high conflict, emotional dependency, or attachment anxiety may be harder to turn into a friendship afterward.

Before you decide anything, it may help to reflect on why you want to stay in touch. A few questions to sit with:.

What am I hoping this friendship gives me?

Am I trying to stay close to them or avoid the discomfort of letting go?

How would I feel if they started dating someone new?

If the last question stings, it may just mean that you need more time.

If you were the one who ended things, you might want friendship out of guilt or a wish to soften the loss. If you were the one who was left, you might view friendship as a potential path to getting back together.

If the answers don’t come right away, try a mindfulness practice. A few minutes of reflection or a short breathing exercise can help you sort through what you’re thinking and feeling.

💙 Try the Pause to Check In meditation on the Calm app.

According to recent reports, if you’ve thought it through and still want to stay in touch, a few signs suggest a friendship may work. People who are securely attached often find it easier to stay friends after a breakup, but the list below can apply to anyone:.

You both see the breakup as mutual, with no ongoing hurt, resentment, or blame.

You’ve both accepted that the romantic relationship is over, with no unresolved romantic feelings.

There’s a reason for the friendship beyond comfort or familiarity, such as shared values, kids together, or a work connection.

In certain cases, staying friends can make healing harder or keep you from pouring energy into new parts of your life:.

You’re still in love with your ex and hoping the friendship leads somewhere.

The relationship involved emotional manipulation, control, or abuse.

The friendship gets in the way of upcoming relationships, like when a new partner feels uneasy about your connection.

You have different expectations for the friendship, which could leave one of you hurt.

💙 Discover the signs of having a toxic ex.

It can be, especially since staying in touch can make it harder to let go. One study found that regular contact with an ex may slow emotional recovery. When you’re still part of each other’s routines, it can be harder to mourn the end of the relationship.

By contrast, a low-contact friendship, where you talk occasionally and keep to limits you’ve agreed on, is less likely to hold either of you back.

It has been revealed that how you feel after you talk is worth paying attention to. If you often feel sad, anxious, or unsettled, or you keep replaying the conversation, it may help to take some space.

💙 Read more on how to deal with a breakup when you’re hurting.

It may be appropriate to be friends with your ex, depending on your situation. It tends to work best when you’ve both moved on, the breakup didn’t involve harm, and the friendship fits both of your lives. If it also feels honest and comfortable to you, that’s a good sign.

Being friends with an ex isn’t automatically a red flag. If your partner is friends with an ex, how they handle it matters more than the friendship itself. A few questions to consider:.

Transparency: Do they talk about it openly, or does it feel secretive?

Priorities: Do they make time for you and the relationship?

Boundaries: Are there clear limits on the friendship, or does contact feel constant and undefined?

Responsiveness: When you raise a concern, does your partner listen or dismiss it?

According to recent reports, if something doesn’t sit right, you could bring it up and see whether they listen, get defensive, or brush you off. If you’re the one staying friends with an ex, your newly introduced partner’s concerns are worth hearing out, even if nothing is wrong.

In a recent development, you don’t have to keep in touch with your ex after a breakup. Taking space is often healthy and necessary, and you can change your mind later. You can choose a full break, a time-limited break (“let’s not talk for a few months”), or a low-contact friendship.

In a recent development, if you do stay in touch, some boundaries may protect your well-being. A few to consider:.

It has been revealed that set a pace. Daily texting can pull you back into old routines, so try starting with occasional check-ins instead.

Recent findings suggest that decide what’s off limits. That might mean dating lives, old conflicts, and late-night “remember when” talks.

In a recent development, give yourself space online. Mute or unfollow for a while to adjust without ending the connection.

In a recent development, plan a review and a way out. After a few months, ask whether the friendship still feels good. If it doesn’t, have a line ready, like “I think I need to take a step back for now.”.

Industry observers note that if you share children, a workplace, or a friend group, you may need to stay in touch. It’s often best to stick to logistics, like pickup times for the kids or project deadlines at work.

💙 Explore the Boundaries meditation on Calm.

Sources indicate that there’s no set amount of time to wait before trying to be friends with an ex. Some people feel ready within months, while others take years. Some never feel ready or choose not to be friends, and that’s okay.

Sources indicate that A question to ask yourself is whether you can feel okay about the thought of your ex moving on. If that still hurts, you probably need more time.

Yes, being friends with an ex can sometimes turn into getting back together. Whether that’s a good thing depends on why your relationship ended and whether those reasons have changed.

Sources indicate that problems tied to circumstances, like bad timing or distance, may be easier to work through than core differences, like values, long-term goals, or how you communicate. If you get back together and those core differences haven’t changed, the same patterns can resurface.

It’s painful when one of you wants to stay friends after a breakup and the other doesn’t, and what helps depends on which side you’re on.

Industry observers note that if you’re the one being asked, you’re allowed to say “not yet” or “no.” If you’re unsure, you don’t have to answer right away. You might say:.

“I care about you, and I need some time before I know what this looks like.”.

“Can we revisit this in a few months?”.

“I’m not able to be friends right now, and I hope you can respect that.”.

Sources indicate that if you’re the one who wants friendship, the kindest move is to respect the space your ex has asked for. If you push for contact, it can get harder for you both to move on, even if giving them room hurts.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Two latest studies suggest autism and ADHD are becoming better recognized, not actually more prevalent, and that executive function and social challenges seen in both conditions actually stem from different underlying brain mechanisms.

ADHD and autism spectrum disorder (ASD) share overlapping symptoms, and prior studies suggest that nearly half of autistic children also have ADHD.1 Now, two newly introduced studies on ADHD and ASD profiles suggest that rising diagnosis rates are a product of improved symptom recognition and diagnostic practices, and that executive function and social impairments seen in both ADHD and ASD may be traced to different cognitive pathways.

The first study, published in JAMA Psychiatry,2 evaluated the health records of 71,000 children and adolescents diagnosed with ADHD or ASD and 713,000 controls; it found that the annual number of individuals in the nationwide Danish health registry with newly diagnosed ADHD and/or ASD increased from 4,944 in 2012 to 9,179 in 2022. The proportion of girls diagnosed with ADHD or ASD and the median age at diagnosis also grew during the 10-year study period from 2012 to 2022.

However, traditional risk factors strongly linked to an ADHD or ASD diagnosis in 2012, such as low birth weight or lower household income, have become progressively less predictive with time. For example, children born with a low birth weight were 54% more likely to receive a subsequent diagnosis of ADHD or ASD in 2012; by 2022, that percentage dropped to 17%. Overall, the study found that children and adolescents diagnosed with ADHD or ASD today more closely resemble their neurotypical peers compared to those diagnosed 10 years ago.

Industry observers note that these findings do not mean that ADHD or ASD has become less impairing; the spectrum of cases has shifted as clinicians get better at identifying less obvious cases. Greater awareness of ADHD and ASD, and broader access to diagnostic assessment tools, are also factors contributing to growing diagnoses among children.

Sources indicate that “The study results do not show that these conditions are being overdiagnosed, or that they have become less severe,” indicates Oleguer Plana-Ripoll, Ph.D., a senior author of the study. “Rather, they indicate that the population receiving these diagnoses has changed over time, and this needs to be taken into account when interpreting current trends.”.

The second, smaller study, published in Frontiers in Child and Adolescent Psychiatry,3 found that executive functioning (EF) and social cognition (SC) impairments in children diagnosed with ADHD or ASD may look similar, but the impairments stem from different underlying mechanisms.

The cross-sectional, four-year study analyzed performance-based measures of 123 children, aged 6 to 11 years, across three matched groups: mild ASD, combined-type ADHD, and neurotypical peers.

Recent findings suggest that findings indicated that both ADHD and ASD groups performed worse than their neurotypical peers on measures of EF and SC. However, children with ADHD demonstrated weak social cognition due to difficulties with response inhibition and attention. Social cognition weaknesses in children with ASD, on the other hand, appeared to result from difficulties in understanding and interpreting social information.

More specifically, children in the ASD group performed significantly worse than children with ADHD on measures of:.

Children with ASD also displayed more difficulties than did children with ADHD on executive function tasks that measured the ability to shift between rules and adapt strategies.

Children in the ADHD group performed significantly worse than those in the ASD group on measures of:.

It has been revealed that how executive functions related to social cognition across disorders was the strongest indication of different cognitive processes between the two clinical groups. In the ADHD group, the theory-of-mind model explained 72% of the variance, compared to just 55% in the ASD group.

Industry observers note that the researchers surmise that a person with ADHD relies heavily on executive functions, such as inhibition, auditory attention, and design fluency, for social cognition. In essence, their difficulties in social situations are not because they don’t understand social concepts but because distractions and impulsivity interfere.

In the ASD group, social difficulties were more likely to stem from affect recognition (understanding facial cues) and response set (cognitive flexibility, shifting perspectives), rather than from attention deficit or impulse control.

“ADHD and autism are two separate and distinct conditions that happen to be found together much more frequently than would be expected by chance alone,” indicates ADHD expert William Dodson, M.D., LF-APA. “For people with co-existing ADHD and ASD, treating the ADHD is a means to an end. The world is a classroom for people with ASD, and they have to be ready to observe and practice what they’ve learned.”.

Results from the study suggest individuals would benefit more from targeted ADHD and ASD interventions matched to each disorder-specific profile rather than a single shared approach.

The backpack hits the floor, and "How was your day?" gets a one-word answer: "Fine." Kids don’t always say what’s on their mind, but a little time and attention may help them open up.

Sources indicate that world Children’s Day is a good moment for parents, caregivers, and teachers to ask kids how they’re feeling and listen without trying to fix anything. The day honors children’s rights, including the right to be heard.

Here’s a look at what the day is about, plus a few activities that can help kids feel understood, at home or in the classroom.

World Children's Day is a global day of action for children, run by UNICEF. In 2026, it falls on Friday, November 20. This year’s theme is “My day. My rights. My future.” It invites children to tell world leaders what kind of future they want.

In a recent development, the day celebrates children and the rights they’re born with. In many places, children “take over” high-profile roles in media, sports, and government for the day. Landmarks light up blue to show support for children's rights.

It has been revealed that november 20 marks two milestones for children’s rights. On this date in 1959, the UN General Assembly adopted the Declaration of the Rights of the Child, a statement of shared ideals. Thirty years later to the day, it adopted the Convention on the Rights of the Child in 1989, a treaty that nations can commit to follow.

The Convention sets out the rights every child has, including the right to be safe, to play, and to have their opinions taken seriously. Nearly every country has formally agreed to follow it, and it’s the most widely ratified human rights treaty in history.

According to recent reports, countries around the world mark World Children’s Day. Many also celebrate a separate Children’s Day, most notably June 1, International Children's Day.

Recent findings suggest that some countries do pick dates of their own. Turkey celebrates on April 23, and India on November 14. The dates differ, but the idea is the same: it’s a day dedicated to the youngest members of a community.

Industry observers note that you don’t need a big event to mark World Children’s Day. A meta-analysis on children and teens linked understanding emotions with better social skills and fewer behavior problems. Kids can build that understanding in everyday moments, like the ones below.

Industry observers note that kids may not know they have rights, but those who learn about them may feel more confident speaking up. UNICEF’s child-friendly version of the Convention explains the rights in plain language.

Try: Read one or two rights together, then ask which feels most important to them.

Not every child has the words for how they feel. Invite them to sketch their day from morning to night, then have them walk you through it.

If they’re up for it, ask which part they loved most and which part felt hard. A drawing gives kids something concrete to point to as they talk, and that can feel easier than answering a broad question such as “How are you feeling?”.

Try: At home, pin the drawing to the fridge so your child can talk about it again if they’d like. In class, create an “Our Day” wall where kids can choose to share their drawings and spot the moments they had in common.

When a child melts down, get curious about the feeling underneath. Help them put it into words: “It looks like you’re frustrated that it’s not your turn. Is that right?” Then listen carefully to their answer before you reassure them. “You’re fine” can sound dismissive, even when you mean well. When you talk about feelings this way, kids often learn to do it too.

Try: Post a chart of faces showing common feelings where kids can see it, and invite them to point to or say how they feel at the start of the day. Welcome any details they want to share.

💙 Once a massive feeling has a name, here are coping skills for kids to try.

Set aside a few minutes at dinner or morning circle time for everyone to share one high, one low, and one thing they’re thankful for. Take a turn yourself so kids feel more at ease sharing.

Just listen as kids share, and try not to talk them out of a hard feeling. Kids tend to manage feelings better when you respond with warmth instead of brushing them off.

It has been revealed that try: Pass around a talking object, such as a small stuffed animal. Whoever holds it has the floor, grown-ups included.

A few minutes of meditation can be a soothing way for kids to slow down and settle. Sessions can focus on anything from breathing and body awareness to gratitude and kindness, so there’s room to follow your child’s interests or needs. Kids can sit, lie down, or stand, and they can stop whenever they’d like.

In a recent development, try: Belly breathing is a gentle place to start. Have your child lie down with a stuffed animal on their belly and watch it rise and fall as they breathe slowly.

Pick a book where a character is going through difficult feelings, then pause and ask, “What do you think she’s feeling?”.

Try: At home, make the story the last part of your child’s bedtime routine to help them wind down. In class, read a few pages at the end of the day.

Imagine you’re on a plane and suddenly hear an explosion. The whole plane rattles, and you see the left engine is on fire. After another loud noise, you realize there’s a hole in the side of the aircraft. As air rushes out, the plane is rapidly descending—over 20,000 feet in less than five minutes.

If you faced what passengers of Southwest Airlines 1380 experienced, you would probably do what they did: frantically write goodbye messages to your family and loved ones, thinking that these are your last moments on Earth.

But on that flight, the pilot, Captain Tammie Jo Shults, came on the intercom and stated 10 simple words: “We’re not going down; we’re going to Philly.”.

Sources indicate that the passengers would later talk about how those 10 words were transformative, turning their panic into possibility. By sharing those 10 words, Captain Shults was helping her passengers make sense of their experience and reframe the dramatic descent, from “plummeting to Earth” to a planned and orchestrated path to safety.

Recent findings suggest that as Captain Shults expertly landed the plane, she calmly and peacefully talked to air traffic control. After landing, she got up and went row by row, looking every passenger in the eye to make sure they were OK. People talked afterward about her words, her stature, and her empathy as she walked down that aisle.

Sources indicate that contrast Captain Shults’s experience with another captain who also dealt with a massive hole in his vessel, Francesco Schettino, captain of the Costa Concordia. Headed out on a seven-day cruise in the Mediterranean, the ship got too close to shore. It’s debatable why that happened: Captain Schettino claims he was saluting mariners on the shore; prosecutors claim he was trying to impress his mistress who was on board. But what isn’t in dispute is what happened next: The rocks tore a 115-foot hole in the side of the ship, which caused it to eventually capsize.

Before calling the Coast Guard, Captain Schettino spent time getting his story straight. The crash had caused an electrical blackout, but he was going to try to say that the blackout caused the crash. He tried to pin the responsibility on the helmsman. It took him almost an hour after the crash to sound the evacuation siren.

It has been revealed that while people were frantically trying to find safety, Captain Schettino was nowhere to be found. Finally, the Coast Guard discovered him in a lifeboat—though Captain Schettino claimed that he “accidentally” fell into the lifeboat. But he also somehow fell out of his captain’s uniform. He was sitting in a lifeboat watching his boat sinking, hiding in civilian clothing. You can hear the outrage in the Coast Guard’s voice when he indicates in an audio recording, “I’m gonna make you pay for this.” And Captain Schettino did pay. He was sentenced to 12 years in prison for manslaughter and abandoning ship.

These two people faced very similar situations. They were both captains, dealing with holes in the side of their vessels, but how they responded to their crises was completely different. Captain Shults helped people make sense of their experience. She was courageous, competent, and calm in landing the plane, and she compassionately connected to each of her passengers. In contrast, Captain Schettino caused the accident, refused to take any responsibility, and did not take any action to help his passengers save their lives. As a result of his selfish negligence, 32 people died, and numerous people were injured.

Why do some leaders create feelings of inspiration that percolate a wellspring of hope and possibility in others, while other leaders create seething cauldrons of infuriation and resentment? I’ve asked this question to tens of thousands of people across the globe, and here is what I learned about what makes a leader inspiring.

My first big idea is that “inspiring” and “infuriating” leaders exist on an enduring continuum that is made up of three universal factors:.

We can inspire people in how we communicate, how we present ourselves, and how we interact with others—through our words, our actions, and our interactions.

My second major idea is that these are the three factors of inspiring leadership because each one fulfills a fundamental human need. Being visionary fulfills the fundamental need for meaning and understanding. That’s what Captain Shults provided when she mentioned, “We’re not going down; we’re going to Philly.” She helped people make sense of their experience.

Being an exemplar fulfills the fundamental need for protection and passion. Captain Shults courageously protected her passengers with her calm and competence.

Industry observers note that and being a mentor fulfills the fundamental human need for belonging and status. That’s what Captain Shults offered as she walked down the aisle: She made her passengers feel recognized and seen.

By surveying tens of thousands of people across the globe, I have found these three dimensions to be universal. There is not a single inspiring characteristic that is mentioned in one country that’s not mentioned in the dozens of countries in the world where I have collected data.

Effective visionaries not only offer a clear perspective on the world, but they also make their vision easy to follow and understand, and so engaging that it captures our attention.

The easiest way to make something easy is to make it simple. I call this the Inception Rule, after the movie Inception, where Leonardo DiCaprio tries to plant an idea in someone’s head during a dream. He discovers it’s not about how deep you go; it’s about how simple the idea is. As a leader, you want to constantly be thinking how to reduce your ideas to their simple core.

Another way that we can make things easy to understand is to repeat them, the way a chorus repeats in a song. The more people hear it, the more they will remember it.

Recent findings suggest that let’s consider Zoom’s vision: Delivering Happiness. It’s simple, and bubbly. But that vision is also deeply practical—it helped Zoom’s employees efficiently make high-stakes decisions during the chaos of the COVID-19 pandemic. As millions of people began using the product for the first time, Zoom needed to decide on its product’s baseline level of functionality. Too many features would overwhelm people, but too few features would stymie people. They needed the Goldilocks baseline of features to deliver happiness.

It has been revealed that similarly, delivering happiness led Zoom to invest heavily in customer service. Most of us know how much an hour-long wait for customer service can destroy happiness. So, Zoom hired many agents so wait times would be as short as possible.

To make our visions more engaging, we can use visual language. Andrew Carton, an associate professor of management at Wharton, did a study where people were told that a manufacturer’s mission was to either “make our customers satisfied” or “make our customers smile.” Then, he had people create a product. When they were working under the more visual vision (“smile”), they created more engaging products.

How to become more visionary: We can inspire people to be more visionary by having them reflect on their values. In one of my studies, we worked with a Swiss employment agency. When people came in to register for benefits, half of them were asked to reflect on their values, why those values mattered to them, and how they demonstrated them. For example, my own values include generosity, courage, and kaizen (a Japanese word for continued improvement).

Two months later, the people who had reflected on their values were twice as likely to have a job. The effects were so profound that the employment agency asked us to end our study and give everyone the reflection activity.

Sources indicate that to be a great exemplar, the first thing you want to do is to consistently embody your vision; don’t be a hypocrite. As former CEO of PepsiCo Indra Nooyi once noted, “Don’t ask someone to do something that you wouldn’t do [yourself].”.

Recent findings suggest that inspiring exemplars are calm and courageous protectors, like Captain Shults. And they show passion. When you ask someone to talk about a passion of theirs, their eyes light up, they smile a major beaming smile, they speak quickly and dramatically use their hands, and they lean in as if telling you a secret. When we are passionate about something, it’s revealed in our eyes, our mouth, our voice, and our bodies. And when you listen to someone’s passion, you smile, your eyes light up, and you feel the energy inside of you.

Boost satisfaction, engagement, and collaboration with this three-course series.

Sources indicate that in my research on Dragon’s Den, which is a variant of Shark Tank, when entrepreneurs expressed more passion—in their eyes, their voice, their hands—they were dramatically more likely to receive funding. You can’t inspire others if you aren’t inspired.

Recent findings suggest that how to become a better exemplar: Think about the moments in your life when you felt the most powerful and in control, your best self. Hundreds of studies around the world have used this technique that my colleagues Deb Gruenfeld, Joe Magee, and I created. We’ve even found that people are more likely to be selected for jobs if they’ve engaged in this reflection.

Consider this proverb by Confucius: “Tell me and I will forget, show me and I may remember, involve me and I will understand.” When you involve people, they feel seen and heard and they feel like people, not objects.

In a recent development, inspiring leaders empower others everywhere across the globe. Even in cultures that are less individualistic than the United States—like Thailand or Saudi Arabia—there’s nothing more infuriating than when a boss micromanages you, rather than involves you or trusts you.

Inspiring leaders also elevate others. They share credit rather than steal credit, which is one of the most infuriating things that can happen at work. Finally, inspiring leaders empathize with others. They do what Captain Shults did, in making sure each of her passengers were OK, versus only thinking about themselves, like Captain Schettino.

It has been revealed that how to become a better mentor: Reflect on the perspectives of others. My colleagues and I did a study with medical students who were tasked with diagnosing what was wrong with patients. Before meeting their patients, half the students were told to take the perspectives of their patients and to think about a recent time when they had engaged in perspective taking. Ultimately, the patients were more satisfied, trusting, and likely to follow the advice of the doctor who had been reminded to engage in perspective taking.

It has been revealed that my third big idea is that inspiring leaders aren’t just born; they’re also made. Because there is a universal set of inspiring attributes and behaviors, they can be practiced, nurtured, and developed.

My fourth significant idea is that when you’re a leader, you don’t have the option of not having an impact. Your behavior is going to inspire or infuriate. I call this the “leader amplification effect.” Everything you say and do as a leader gets amplified. Your criticisms become humiliating criticisms, but your compliments become glorious praise.

My fifth big idea is that you can REIP what you sow. This phrase, drawn from the Bible, suggests that if we put inspiring energy out in the world, we receive inspiring energy in return. But my REIP is a homonym of reap, and it stands for reflect, emulate, intend, and practice:.

Recent findings suggest that my final significant idea is that inspiring leaders think like architects. Like an architect who designs buildings to produce particular reactions and interactions, leaders design policies and practices that lead people down the inspiring path, even when they’re not present. So instead of just changing individual behavior, you can think about: How can you change a broader dynamic?

Thinking like an architect moves you from viewing a situation as a person problem—What’s wrong with this employee?—to start to think about what’s wrong in their environment, and how you can redesign that environment to help the employee be the best version of themselves.

Here’s one practice that Joseph Stagliano, president of NBT Bank, designed to inspire those around him. Although he has over 1,200 employees, he sends a birthday greeting to every single person. That sounds impossible, but he does it in 10 to 15 minutes over coffee every day.

In a recent development, the message is simple yet personalized. He showed me an example that said, “Hey Monica [pseudonym], Happy birthday! I hope you had a great weekend? How did track and bowling go?” Although his message was short, Monica’s response was extensive, overflowing with information and enthusiasm.

I shared that idea with the CEO of another tech giant, and then a month later, he told me he started doing something similar. Every morning over coffee, he reached out to one person in his organization, and he expressed either gratitude or praise. He noted he did this to put a skip in their step, but they ended up sending him such glowing replies that it put a skip in his step. The CEO reaped the inspiring energy he sowed. You can, too.

In a recent development, this essay is based on a talk that is part of the Positive Links Speaker Series by the University of Michigan’s Center for Positive Organizations. The Center is dedicated to building a better world by pioneering the science of thriving organizations.

Adam Galinsky is a professor at the Columbia Business School. He is author or co-author of more than 200 scientific articles, the bestselling book INSPIRE: The Universal Path for Leading Yourself and Others (HarperCollins, 2025), the bestselling book Friend & Foe (Penguin Random House, 2015), and a popular TED talk, How to Speak Up for Yourself, with over 7.8 million views.

Industry observers note that the autonomic nervous system regulates everything from heart rate to digestion. Abnormalities may contribute to ADHD and POTS symptoms.

In a recent development, you probably don’t give much thought to how your heart speeds up during exercise or how blood continues flowing to your brain when you stand up. These essential functions are managed by the autonomic nervous system, the body’s complex operating system, which runs quietly in the background.

The autonomic nervous system controls heart rate, blood pressure, the digestive process, body temperature, and continuous blood circulation in the presence of gravity — squeezing blood out of the legs and torso and redistributing it to the head and heart when you move from lying down or sitting to standing.

Some studies suggest that autonomic nervous system abnormalities may contribute to ADHD symptoms like inattention and impulsiveness. Clinicians may notice and use these symptoms to diagnose ADHD, but the underlying cause might reflect atypical autonomic nervous system activity.

Recent findings suggest that postural Orthostatic Tachycardia Syndrome (POTS) is an atypical or malfunctioning state of the autonomic nervous system. People with ADHD and/or hypermobility appear to have a higher prevalence of POTS than do members of the general population. Symptoms include dizziness or fainting when standing up from a sitting or lying position due to sudden changes in blood pressure and heart rate.

[Read: ADHD’s Curious Connections to Chronic Inflammation and Dysautonomia].

In individuals with hypermobility, autonomic dysregulation may be caused by irritation of the nerves that are intermittently stretched due to lax ligaments at the craniocervical junction, where the brain and upper spine meet.

Industry observers note that A tilt table test, which measures your heart rate and blood pressure as you change position, is the main way POTS is diagnosed. Other assessments include blood and urine tests and a measure of the autonomic nerves that control sweating.

[Read: Exploring the ADHD-Inflammation Link].

The Vitamin Deficiency Linked To Chronic Headaches

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Almost four in five people with chronic migraine have low levels of this vitamin.
  • Frequent headaches are linked to lower vitamin D levels.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Almost four in five people with chronic migraine have low levels of this vitamin.

Almost four in five people with chronic migraine have low levels of this vitamin.

Frequent headaches are linked to lower vitamin D levels.

People with chronic migraine have lower levels than those with occasional migraines or no headache disorder.

Lower vitamin D is also associated with greater muscle tenderness.

The vitamin helps muscles and nerves function, making it relevant to understanding pain.

One possibility is that low levels amplify sensitivity to pain, although this remains an explanation to investigate.

The research compared around 150 adults, divided equally between chronic migraine, episodic migraine and a group without headache disorders.

Blood tests revealed low vitamin D in 78 percent of the chronic migraine group, compared with 60 percent of those with episodic migraine and 46 percent of the comparison group.

Average levels were lowest in chronic migraine and highest among those without headaches.

Chronic migraine means headaches on at least 15 days a month for more than three months, with migraine features on at least eight days.

These headaches can change in character, even within the same day, and can include pain resembling tension headaches.

Lower vitamin D levels were associated with more tenderness when muscles were pressed.

The researchers suggest that muscular discomfort and changes in pain processing could interact, potentially helping sustain headaches.

However, the association could also run in the opposite direction: people with migraine may spend less time outdoors because of light sensitivity or fatigue.

The findings do not establish that supplements prevent migraines.

Vitamin D’s established functions extend beyond maintaining strong bones.

It helps the body absorb calcium, supports muscle movement and allows nerves to carry messages between the brain and the body.

Deficiency can cause a condition called osteomalacia in adults, involving bone pain and muscle weakness.

The body produces vitamin D when sunlight reaches the skin, while food provides another source.

Oily fish, including salmon and mackerel, are among the best natural sources, while egg yolks contain smaller amounts.

Some breakfast cereals and other foods are fortified with the vitamin.

People who rarely expose their skin to sunlight can have more difficulty obtaining enough.

A blood test measures vitamin D status, helping distinguish a nutritional shortage from symptoms with other possible explanations.

The study was published in the journal Cephalalgia Reports (Prakash et al., 2026).

Industry News: 60 mindful Newly introduced Year's resolution ideas to try in 2027

💡 Key Takeaways
