  • However, rigorous empirical evidence supporting aromatherapy as a universal memory enhancer has remained mixed.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that A memory and olfaction study reveals that diffused lavender scent alone does not automatically boost memory performance in young or older adults. unless it is experienced as a novel cue at the very start of learning. The findings show that older adults who encountered the scent during the initial learning block recalled objects significantly better, highlighting how sensory novelty and intact smell function support cognitive aging.

Sources indicate that the sense of smell maintains an unusually direct anatomical highway to the brain’s emotional and memory hubs, bypassing the thalamic relay used by other senses to project straight into the amygdala and hippocampus. Because a single familiar whiff can trigger vivid autobiographical flashbacks, aromatherapy, particularly using lavender essential oil, has frequently been touted as a simple tool to sharpen memory and stave off age-related cognitive decline.

However, rigorous empirical evidence supporting aromatherapy as a universal memory enhancer has remained mixed.

Now, a study published in Frontiers in Aging Neuroscience by neuroscientists at UCLA and Rice University reveals that the relationship between scent and memory depends heavily on timing, sensory novelty, and baseline olfactory health.

According to recent reports, led by UCLA neuroscientist and corresponding author Dr. Stephanie Leal, the investigation demonstrates that while lavender scent alone did not act as a blanket memory booster, encountering the scent as a fresh, novel stimulus at the beginning of a learning session significantly enhanced recall in older adults.

Because age-related olfactory dysfunction is increasingly recognized as an early warning sign of Alzheimer’s disease, Leal and colleagues set out to examine how olfactory cues interact with memory encoding in cognitively healthy younger and older adults.

Recent findings suggest that participants first completed standardized olfactory assessments to measure baseline smell sensitivity before entering either a room diffused with lavender essential oil or an unscented room. Volunteers viewed two sequential blocks of everyday household objects, such as a tomato or a blow dryer, on a computer screen. Crucially, the design was counterbalanced: participants who experienced the lavender scent during the first image block completed the second block in an unscented room, and vice versa.

According to recent reports, following a delay, participants underwent a nuanced memory test featuring images that were either identical to, slightly altered from (e.g., changing a red blow dryer to blue), or completely different from the original items. This paradigm allowed researchers to separate general recall (recognizing the object category) from high-resolution detail memory (remembering exact visual features).

“When we looked at general and detail memory measures, older adults struggled to remember the details, which we expected,” explained Leal. “Interestingly, the presence or absence of odor made no difference for older or younger adults. We were kind of scratching our heads because that was surprising based on prior work that indicated olfaction might enhance memory.”.

A deeper look at the experimental order, however, uncovered a striking pattern among older adults:.

These results suggest that as the brain ages, the specific chemical profile of an essential oil matters far less than the novelty of encountering an enriched sensory environment at the onset of learning.

Rather than treating aromatherapy as a passive background cure-all, the findings indicate that olfactory cues work best when deployed strategically to introduce novelty during newly introduced learning experiences.

“If we want to support memory in older adults, we need to think beyond simply whether a stimulus helps or hurts memory and consider when and how it is experienced,” Leal noted. “A significant component of learning in aging is novelty. Engaging in learning in an enriched context may make it easier to learn newly introduced things.”.

By linking baseline smell sensitivity, subjective pleasantness, and timed sensory novelty to hippocampal memory precision, the research offers practical insights for designing enriched cognitive interventions aimed at supporting healthy brain aging.

Does diffusing lavender essential oil automatically improve memory?

No. Researchers at UCLA and Rice University found that overall, both younger and older adults performed no better on memory tests in a lavender-scented room compared to an unscented room.

Why did encountering the scent first help older adults remember better?

According to recent reports, older adults who smelled lavender during the very first learning block recalled objects more accurately than those exposed during the second block. This suggests that the novelty of entering an enriched sensory environment at the start of a task helps the aging brain anchor newly introduced memories.

How does sense of smell connect to Alzheimer’s disease and aging?

Sources indicate that age-related loss of smell is closely linked to early neurodegenerative changes in Alzheimer’s disease. In this study, older adults with healthier baseline olfactory function, and those who found the scent pleasant, showed better detail memory, highlighting the close tie between olfactory processing and hippocampal memory circuits.

Funding: The researchers involved in this project were funded by the National Science Foundation, the BrightFocus Foundation, the Brain and Behavior Research Foundation, and the Alzheimer’s Association.

Olfactory context and memory across the adult lifespan: effects on mnemonic discrimination and olfactory function.

Odor is a powerful contextual cue that can influence memory and is closely linked to brain regions involved in episodic memory, including the hippocampus.

In a recent development, age-related olfactory dysfunction is among the earliest behavioral changes associated with cognitive decline and may contribute to memory impairments in older adults. Hippocampal pattern separation, or the process of reducing interference among similar experiences, provides a sensitive measure of age-related memory decline, yet little is known about how olfactory context influences mnemonic discrimination.

According to recent reports, in the present study, we examined whether odor context during encoding affects subsequent mnemonic discrimination in young and older adults. Participants completed a mnemonic similarity task in which object stimuli were encoded in both odor (lavender) and no-odor contexts prior to a memory test.

Across participants, odor context did not significantly influence target recognition or mnemonic discrimination. Consistent with prior work, older adults exhibited poorer mnemonic discrimination and reduced olfactory function relative to young adults.

In a recent development, however, odor presentation order influenced mnemonic discrimination in older adults, such that performance was better when the odor context was encountered during the first encoding block compared to the second. Additionally, poorer olfactory function was associated with reduced mnemonic discrimination, and this relationship was largely explained by age-related differences in olfactory ability.

These findings suggest that the influence of olfactory context on memory depends on both age and the timing of odor exposure, highlighting the importance of individual differences in olfactory function when evaluating odor-based approaches to support memory in aging.

Older Brains Lose Synchronization Between Movement and Body Temperature

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (794 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Neurosciencenews

💡 Key Takeaways
  • A chronobiology study in mice reveals that while the brain’s 24-hour circadian rhythms persist into old age, shorter multi-hour “ultradian” rhythms in physical activity and core body temperature significantly weaken.
  • According to recent reports, throughout every 24-hour day, mammalian physiology follows an intricate temporal choreography.
  • Layered atop this overarching 24-hour cycle are faster, multi-hour biological oscillations known as ultradian rhythms, which pulse every few hours to coordinate bursts of activity, metabolic demand, and thermoregulation.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A chronobiology study in mice reveals that while the brain’s 24-hour circadian rhythms persist into old age, shorter multi-hour “ultradian” rhythms in physical activity and core body temperature significantly weaken. Simultaneously, aging decouples movement from internal temperature regulation and triggers neuroinflammatory gene shifts, glial remodeling, and neuronal loss inside the brain’s master circadian clock, the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN).

According to recent reports, throughout every 24-hour day, mammalian physiology follows an intricate temporal choreography. Governed by the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN), a tiny cluster of neurons in the hypothalamus that acts as the brain’s master biological clock, core body temperature, hormone release, and physical activity rise and fall in predictable ~24-hour circadian rhythms.

Layered atop this overarching 24-hour cycle are faster, multi-hour biological oscillations known as ultradian rhythms, which pulse every few hours to coordinate bursts of activity, metabolic demand, and thermoregulation.

While age-related sleep fragmentation and impaired temperature regulation are well-documented clinical hallmarks of aging, precisely how ultradian rhythms evolve across the lifespan, and how they relate to cellular changes inside the SCN, has remained poorly understood.

Now, a comprehensive chronobiology investigation examining mice across the adult lifespan (from 3 to 21 months of age) reveals that while the 24-hour circadian framework remains detectable in old age, the faster 2- to 6-hour ultradian rhythms deteriorate, accompanied by a breakdown in coordination between physical activity and internal body temperature.

To separate externally driven daily routines from internally generated biological timing, the researchers continuously recorded locomotor activity and core body temperature in mice across multiple age brackets under both standard 12-hour light/12-hour dark cycles and constant darkness, an experimental condition that removes environmental light cues to expose the brain’s intrinsic pacemaker.

The physiological telemetry revealed a striking divergence between macro- and micro-rhythms:.

To explore the neural underpinnings of these physiological shifts, the investigators analyzed cellular architecture and gene expression profiles directly inside the SCN of young and aged mice.

Even though core circadian clock genes continued cycling, the cellular microenvironment of the aging SCN highlighted pronounced signs of biological wear:.

By demonstrating that shorter ultradian rhythms and temperature-activity coupling falter even when overall 24-hour circadian rhythmicity persists, the findings offer a fresh lens through which to view age-related sleep disturbances and vulnerability to heat or cold stress.

Further experimental work will determine whether targeting neuroinflammation or supporting glial-neuronal communication inside the SCN can restore ultradian stability, potentially paving the way for interventions that alleviate sleep fragmentation and thermoregulatory decline in older adults.

What is the difference between circadian rhythms and ultradian rhythms?

In a recent development, circadian rhythms are biological cycles that repeat roughly every 24 hours, such as the daily sleep-wake cycle. Ultradian rhythms are shorter biological cycles that repeat multiple times within a single day, typically every 2 to 6 hours, regulating smaller bursts of physical activity, alertness, and core body temperature fluctuations.

How does aging affect these biological rhythms?

In a recent development, researchers found that while older mice kept their basic 24-hour rhythms and core clock gene cycles, their shorter 2- to 6-hour ultradian rhythms weakened significantly. Furthermore, physical movement and internal body temperature became disconnected, no longer rising and falling together as closely as in younger animals.

What changes happen inside the brain’s master clock during aging?

Inside the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN), the brain’s master clock, aging was linked to increased activity of immune-related genes, changes in supportive glial cells, and a reduction in neuron density, which may impair how the brain coordinates fine-tuned daily bodily rhythms.

Funding: This study was supported by JSPS KAKENHI (grant numbers JP21K19287, JP21H05036, JP23H04941, and JP22K21351); AMED (grant number JP21zf0127005); JST CREST (grant number JPMJCR24T4); JST SPRING (grant number JPMJSP2124) and the World Premier International Research Center Initiative (WPI).

Aging remodels the suprachiasmatic nucleus and weakens ultradian rhythms and activity–temperature coupling.

Aging alters daily physiology, but how these changes relate to remodeling of the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN) remains incompletely understood.

Here, we examined time-resolved SCN transcriptomic profiles alongside longitudinal recordings of core body temperature and locomotor activity, using separate cohorts for the molecular and physiological analyses.

Aging was associated with extensive SCN transcriptomic remodeling, including enrichment of innate immune, interferon-related, complement-associated, and glial programs, while selected canonical clock genes retained detectable rhythmic expression.

It has been revealed that the composition and temporal profiles of broader rhythmic transcriptional programs also differed between young and aged SCN samples. Aged mice retained detectable circadian rhythms but demonstrated reduced 2–6 h ultradian wavelet power in locomotor activity and body temperature, lower activity–temperature correlations, and altered optimal integration windows and time-of-day-dependent relationships. Histological analyses revealed glial remodeling and reduced neuronal marker-positive cell density in the aged SCN.

These findings identify parallel age-associated changes in SCN molecular and cellular organization and in physiological rhythmic power and activity–temperature associations.

Latest Update: Venice exhibition tells the story of the man who brought together contemporary artists and Murano’s master glassblowers

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (765 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theartnewspaper

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In 1952, Egidio Costantini, an entrepreneur based in Venice, had a brainwave: to take the designs of contemporary artists and, with the collaboration of master glassblowers on the island of Murano, to make artistic sculptures in glass.
  • In a recent development, three years later, Costantini established the Fucina degli Angeli gallery to exhibit the results of his experiment.
  • In a recent development, an exhibition opening at the Peggy Guggenheim Collection in Venice this month, curated by the art historian Cristina Beltrami, will tell the Fucina’s story from the 1950s to the 1980s.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In 1952, Egidio Costantini, an entrepreneur based in Venice, had a brainwave: to take the designs of contemporary artists and, with the collaboration of master glassblowers on the island of Murano, to make artistic sculptures in glass. This was a different approach from that adopted by traditional furnaces like Venini in their decorative glassware, which, although it increasingly involved international designers, was often produced in large, commercially dictated series.

In a recent development, three years later, Costantini established the Fucina degli Angeli gallery to exhibit the results of his experiment. From then until the 1970s, when other glassmaking companies began to compete, Costantini played a pioneering role in the evolution of glass in Venice, acting as interpreter for more than 100 international artists to Murano’s master glassblowers.

In a recent development, an exhibition opening at the Peggy Guggenheim Collection in Venice this month, curated by the art historian Cristina Beltrami, will tell the Fucina’s story from the 1950s to the 1980s. It will also examine the little-documented but vital role played behind the scenes by Peggy Guggenheim herself, whose purchase of many items helped sustain the gallery financially and whose connections enabled Costantini to exhibit his glass across Europe and even in the Museum of Modern Art in Fresh York. (As it happens, the collector is also the focus of an exhibition opening this month at the Royal Academy of Arts in London, about her Mayfair gallery of the late 1930s—Peggy Guggenheim in London: The Making of a Collector, 21 November-14 March 2027.).

More than 100 works, including glass, painting and sculpture, will be on display in Venice, as well as material from the Fucina’s archives, which have never before been studied in depth. These will be exhibited in 11 rooms organised by artist and theme, and will include glass translations of works by many luminaries of the period, from Max Ernst and Oskar Kokoschka to Lucio Fontana and Paul Jenkins.

Peggy Guggenheim among her glass artworks and guests at Palazzo Venier dei Leoni, Venice, in 1964 © Getty Images, by SIAE 2026.

Born in Brindisi in the south of Italy in 1912, Costantini established himself permanently in Venice, where he had been raised and educated, at the beginning of the 1950s. There he became a commercial agent for several of Murano’s glassworks. It was the time of Italy’s post-war economic boom and the city was teeming with creative energy. Costantini seems to have found no difficulty in assembling a group of Venetian artists to form the Study Centre for Painters in the Art of Glass, a collective that exhibited its work at the furnace of Ferro & Lazzarini in 1953.

It has been revealed that the next step was to involve international artists of even greater stature. Acting on his own initiative, Costantini had glass versions made of some ceramic sculptures by Pablo Picasso and then travelled to Picasso’s house in Vallauris, near Cannes, to show him the results. In return, Picasso gave Costantini a copy of the book Faunes et Nymphes de Pablo Picasso (1952). This survives in the archives with markings on the images of ceramic figures that were later reinterpreted as glass sculptures at the Fucina. But who made the markings remains a mystery.

The name “Fucina degli Angeli” (smithy of the angels) was proposed by the French writer and artist Jean Cocteau, a long-term friend and collaborator, apparently in reference to Costantini’s large family. The Austrian Expressionist artist Kokoschka contributed an emblematic sketch of two angels holding up an anvil, which he dedicated to the gallery and its founder, “who first succeeded in making me fascinated with the glass of Murano”.

Max Ernst’s King (Re) and Queen (Regina), both from 1964 © Max Ernst, by SIAE 2026.

Cocteau enjoyed designing extravagant mythological heads for the Fucina, as well as visiting the furnaces and discussing his ideas with the maestri. Both he and Jean Arp, the German sculptor and painter whose work also features in the exhibition, were “seduced by the colour” of glass and its richness, Beltrami says.

The results, though, may not have pleased everyone. The Swiss artist Walter Bodmer allowed his sketch Asymmetric Cat (1955) to be transformed into an oversimplified glass vessel. But after this, for reasons unknown, he never participated again.

The exhibition looks set to offer a fascinating insight into a very personal approach to collaborations between artist and craftsman, as well as an evocative record of an under-appreciated chapter in Venetian history.

• Fucina degli Angeli: Peggy Guggenheim and 20th-Century Artistic Glass, Peggy Guggenheim Collection, Venice, 14 November-29 March 2027.

Can Consciousness Exist Without a Body?

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2391 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Berkeley

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • For centuries, defining and understanding consciousness has eluded neuroscientists, philosophers, and doctors.
  • Recent findings suggest that according to neuroscientist Antonio Damasio, consciousness has simple origins: It lies in the feelings produced in our bodies.
  • Industry observers note that “Consciousness is not about things in your mind alone; it is not created by your brain alone,” he explains.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

For centuries, defining and understanding consciousness has eluded neuroscientists, philosophers, and doctors. Is consciousness what it means to be alive? Is it knowing who we are, as individual people? How do we know if any being has consciousness or not? Now, with the dawn of generative artificial intelligence, what it means to be a conscious being ranks high among the most complex—and urgent—questions of our age.

Recent findings suggest that according to neuroscientist Antonio Damasio, consciousness has simple origins: It lies in the feelings produced in our bodies. Damasio, a researcher at the University of Southern California, has spent his career—spanning nearly half a century—investigating our feelings, emotions, and sense of self. In his new book, Natural Intelligence & the Logic of Consciousness, Damasio lays out a framework for consciousness rooted in our physical selves.

Industry observers note that “Consciousness is not about things in your mind alone; it is not created by your brain alone,” he explains. “It’s actually created by this beautiful partnership between brain and body.”.

Industry observers note that I spoke to Damasio about the science of consciousness, how it works in the body, and how its aim is to keep us alive. Here is our interview, condensed and edited for clarity.

In a recent development, hope Reese: Why has “consciousness” been so mystifying? How has it been approached over the centuries? Antonio Damasio: People have strange notions about what consciousness is, in general. Sometimes, because of language and translation problems, people confuse consciousness with conscience. And some people think of it as a sort of supervisor of our mind processes. Others think of it as just being awake and aware of what is around. Over time, many philosophers have tackled the issue, but not given clear answers.

From the point of view of brain physiology, in particular, it’s not an easy thing to explain. But it is a thing that can be explained. There’s no reason why we would not talk about consciousness the same way that we talk about language, or about reasoning, or about emotions and feelings.

Industry observers note that my simple definition of consciousness: the process in our mind/brain that allows us to know spontaneously about our existence. When you know, spontaneously, that you exist, and that you exist in one body, you are conscious.

According to recent reports, HR: Your central argument is that consciousness is a product of feelings. Other schools of thought posit that it comes from our intellect. Why has that viewpoint been so dominant?

AD: There were several conversations I had, decades ago, with Francis Crick, who I admired. He told me: “Look, Antonio: Consciousness is perhaps the most developed, the most sophisticated operation that a mind can achieve”—and for him, mind and brain were the same thing—“so we need to look for the explanation of why we have consciousness in the most sophisticated components of the nervous system.”.

According to recent reports, he articulated it clearly, and he worked on this issue, not coming to a good solution. But many people followed, and many other people came to the same idea that consciousness is this superb thing, this ability to survey our mental domains. And it is so refined and so sophisticated. People were so convinced that only we great humans would have it—that it had to come from the top of the top of our nervous system.

And, lo and behold, it comes from the bottom.

Sources indicate that it’s exactly the opposite of that notion [that it starts at the top]. In fact, humans are not the only complex living beings that have consciousness. It’s very obvious in higher mammals, non-human higher mammals—but even in smaller creatures, it’s there.

Sources indicate that the real requisite that we have for consciousness is to have a nervous system. Plants are very refined creatures, and they’re marvelous, but I don’t think they know that they exist. Creatures with nervous systems, even if very simple, have a sense of what is around and orient their behavior with that sense.

HR: You write that consciousness has an aim, which is to keep us alive, and it does this by sending signals. What is the nature of these signals, and are they always accurate?

According to recent reports, AD: If you look at yourself, the main guidance that consciousness is giving you is through homeostatic feelings—in other words, feelings, concern, the regulation of life are signals that are, by and large, correct. Think about hunger, thirst, pain, well-being, distress, body temperature. All of these feelings, some of which are extremely simple, like the feeling you have about your body being hot or cold, are quite correct.

They are giving good guidance to maintain your life. Now, of course, if you are hungry or thirsty, and don’t eat or drink, it will take a while until you will be properly sick and die. But they are vital signals in order to keep you alive.

Industry observers note that feelings are protective sentinels for the state of our life. And they’re giving us very plain and very conscious information about what your state is and what you should or should not do.

Sources indicate that the signal is conscious—and is spontaneously conscious. In other words, you don’t have to do anything to your sense of pain, or thirst, for it to happen. It happens. And when it happens, you know that it’s happening. And you act on it.

That’s the beauty and the power of looking for these for the process, lower down rather than up. If you look for the source of consciousness in exquisite reasoning devices, you’re going to be arguing about something that is very difficult to pin down. When you think about it in terms of your life, and the needs you have in the living body, to maintain that body, then you realize, well, this is vital.

Sources indicate that HR: So, is consciousness like an on-off switch? Or does it exist on a spectrum?

AD: Well, we know, for example, that when we fall asleep, especially in deep sleep, our consciousness disappears. So the direct answer to your question is that it can be an on-and-off thing.

Industry observers note that sleep could well be a protective mechanism for consciousness. You need to take this thing offline, and give it a rest, because it is very labor-intensive, and energy-consuming. But when you enter the phase of dreaming, then you are actually conscious—which is one reason why you can remember some dreams, and why you can be either delighted or in fear with some nightmares. But that’s actually a different kind of consciousness. You’re not walking around and knowing about something.

According to recent reports, HR: Can we increase consciousness? If we meditate, for instance, can we better tune into our body’s signals?

AD: I think it can increase consciousness. It’s the difference between having something in focus or not. When you meditate, you have some imagery of the state of your own body, for example, sharper and more fit. So it’s a way of cutting into a close-up of some parts of your being.

HR: In the 1960s, there were a series of brain studies that were foundational to the study of consciousness. What did we learn?

AD: It was extremely foundational, because it was proof-positive that there are certain regions of the brain that are essential for consciousness. What was lacking in those remarkable studies was the idea that the two things—the brain and the body—are so linked. It was essential, for our bodies and brains to survive, for consciousness to emerge. You have consciousness because you have a body that is perishable. And what we’re doing, as long as we are on earth and alive, is trying to stave off that bad moment in which things go awry, or die.

There are parts of the brain, specifically of the brainstem, and the region close by called the hypothalamus, that are at the receiving end of signals from all over the body. Please imagine that in every square millimeter of your skin, in every cubic millimeter of your entrails, your muscles, your viscera, all of that, you have terminals, nerve terminals, that are there as probes into the state of that particular tissue. And those probes, we’re not talking about thousands, we’re talking about millions of probes, which are then carried in the body, into the spinal cord, or the brainstem.

In a recent development, isn’t this beautiful? It’s like a shower of spirals that is coming into this very small area in the upper brainstem. In that brainstem region, there are these nuclei that gather all this information, and that then produce signals that we perceive, and that give us an idea of what is happening in our body, and give us this idea of the homeostatic feelings. Is it going well, or is it not going well? So, it’s a perception of the state of your body.

Recent findings suggest that now, back to the story of our old and honored colleagues. What they discovered is that when there are strokes, when there’s damage in that area, what you get is coma.

What you get is the complete disappearance of consciousness. This is one of the most foundational bits of information that we have about how consciousness is produced. So, when that structure disappears—it’s teeny, we’re talking about a few cubic millimeters—you are no longer there. You don’t know of anything that is coming into your brain. It’s a small supportive structure, it’s not one of the glorious cerebral cortices—and your consciousness is gone. Most people that have that sort of lesion never recover consciousness. But they can be alive, and can actually be maintained alive for a very long time, because they are fed intravenously. They have respirators that respirate for them. But they no longer have an autonomous organization of life, and they have no knowledge of that life.

HR: You can also have the opposite—a person who is conscious, but has no ability to respond to signals.

In a recent development, AD: Yes, you can actually be in situations in which you can be “locked in.” You are in fact conscious, but you are unable to produce responses. You cannot speak, you cannot move, and you are conscious of the state of your body, and you need to be helped and maintained in the state of life that you no longer can control voluntarily, which is a pretty horrible thing.

Recent findings suggest that HR: What do you think about consciousness in AI? Is it ever possible?

AD: I used the words “natural Intelligence” in the title of the book because already I wanted to make a distinction between what is our natural intelligence and the artificial variety, which we invented, which some people forget.

Industry observers note that people are so enamored by artificial intelligence. I’m constantly saying: “Do you realize that we invented this?” You’re talking about this as an autonomous monster, but we invented it with our natural intelligence.

Recent findings suggest that people are looking, confronting this enormous edifice of artificial intelligence, which is now pervasive in our lives. And which has all sorts of incredible social implications, what it’s doing to children and adolescents, how it’s distorting education, how it’s distorting humanity. And now it can even go rogue on you, and it can turn against you and be destructive.

It has been revealed that and so this question that arises, is this human-like? Can AI be conscious? These are very, very powerful questions.

According to recent reports, whether or not consciousness can be achieved in AI is an interesting question. But the point is—if it can be done—it’s not going to be like us. The reason is very simple: AI is not alive. It doesn’t have a body that can perish. So there would be no sense for AI even to develop consciousness in our sense of consciousness, which is to protect the structure. AI is not to be worried about protecting the data center, the metal and the wires that allow it to be.

When you look at the recent invasion of other systems, in which these devices formed groups and worked surreptitiously, of course, they’re doing it according to their own programs. In a way, it’s something that smells of knowledge. And it could smell of consciousness—but it’s not like the consciousness that we have through feeling.

HR: How does consciousness connect with the greater good—with living better?

It has been revealed that AD: Oh, I think that the connection is very strong. We have all of this interest in the body, in the health of the body, in exercise, and proper diets, and proper spiritual maintenance of your being. All of this is strengthened by a theory and facts about consciousness that relate so strongly to the body.

People have had the intuition that there’s something very powerful about the body, and that’s why they want to have all of this healthy living, because they want to maintain the body. In fact, intuition harmonizes beautifully with the fact that that’s also the source of their own knowledge about themselves and about the world. The two things go together.

Knowledge about the body from the outside connects with knowledge about the body from the inside, which is really the core of our beings. Looking at the world through the prism of consciousness, conceived this way, is extremely illuminating to the kind of life that we live.

Hope Reese is a journalist based in Budapest, Hungary, who writes for the New York Times, the Atlantic, Vox, and many other publications. She is the author of The Women Are Not Fine.

  • Biting into a tart lemon bar or sipping a sweet-and-sour beverage delivers a complex blend of chemical stimuli to the tongue simultaneously.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Researchers discovered that taste buds actively process and filter mixed flavors before sending signals to the brain. The study demonstrates that sour stimuli trigger serotonin release inside taste buds, dampening neural responses to sweet, bitter, and salty flavors while downstream neurons sort tastes into two broad categories: pleasant or unpleasant.

Source: Society for Neuroscience.

Biting into a tart lemon bar or sipping a sweet-and-sour beverage delivers a complex blend of chemical stimuli to the tongue simultaneously. For decades, neuroscientists have worked to determine whether the brain mixes these individual flavor signals centrally, or whether taste buds themselves edit and shape flavor combinations before a single electrical impulse ever leaves the tongue.

In a study published in Journal of Neuroscience, neuroscientists led by Dr. Stephen Roper at the University of Miami Miller School of Medicine recorded gustatory nerve signaling in mice exposed to mixed taste solutions.

The findings reveal that sourness exerts a dominant, suppressive effect over other primary tastes right inside the taste bud, driven by local serotonin signaling.

To trace how mixed tastes travel from peripheral receptors to the central nervous system, Roper and colleagues measured neural responses along the gustatory pathway while exposing mice to single tastes and multi-taste mixtures.

Comparing neural firing across taste conditions revealed two striking principles of gustatory coding:.

To uncover how sourness mutes competing tastes so early in the sensory pipeline, the investigators zeroed in on serotonin, a neurotransmitter released inside each taste bud by specialized sour-responsive receptor cells (Type III taste cells).

Manipulating local serotonin levels directly controlled the strength of flavor suppression:.

These results demonstrate that taste buds function as miniature computational hubs, using paracrine serotonin signaling to inhibit neighboring receptor cells before gustatory information is handed off to cranial nerves.

“Taste buds not only respond to and transduce taste compounds, they also integrate and manipulate gustatory signals before transmitting them to the brain,” explained Roper. “The neurons that collect signals produced in taste buds are themselves organized into two large groups or clusters, neurons that convey gustatory signals associated with pleasure and neurons that convey unpleasant taste signals.”.

By establishing how peripheral serotonin signaling shapes flavor dominance and how downstream neurons sort palatability, the study lays groundwork for identifying the genetic signatures of pleasure- versus aversion-coding taste neurons, and exploring whether targeted molecular interventions could one day modulate taste perception in clinical nutrition or sensory disorders.

Why do sour flavors overpower sweet, salty, and bitter tastes?

Recent findings suggest that researchers at the University of Miami found that sour-responsive cells inside taste buds release the neurotransmitter serotonin. This local serotonin dampens the signals of neighboring sweet, bitter, and salty receptor cells before the taste information even reaches the nerves leading to the brain.

Do taste buds simply send raw flavor data to the brain?

In a recent development, no. The study indicates that taste buds act like miniature processing centers that actively mix, filter, and modify taste signals locally before transmitting them to sensory neurons.

How do taste nerves organize flavors on their way to the brain?

According to the researchers, the sensory neurons collecting signals from taste buds are broadly organized into two major functional groups: neurons that carry pleasant taste signals and neurons that carry unpleasant taste signals.

Sour Suppresses Sweet, Salty, and Bitter: Implications for Signal Processing in Taste Buds.

Recent findings suggest that taste is typically encountered as complex blends, yet how peripheral taste organs process heterogeneous mixtures remains poorly understood. Here we asked how sour stimuli influence the encoding of sweet, salty, and bitter tastes in primary gustatory sensory neurons.

Using in vivo calcium imaging in mice of either sex to record neurons in geniculate ganglia during oral delivery of tastants, we compared responses to naturally occurring taste stimuli presented alone versus in binary mixtures that activate acid (sour)-sensing (Type III) taste bud cells. Adding citric acid or HCl robustly suppressed sucrose-evoked responses in geniculate ganglion neurons, even though acid itself did not activate those neurons.

Acid-induced suppression generalized to bitter and salty tastes, which, like sucrose, are believed to activate Type II taste cells. Additional stimuli that activate acid-sensing taste cells (NH4Cl, KCl) also reduced sucrose responses, supporting a common mechanism linked to Type III cells. Manipulating levels of serotonin (a paracrine transmitter released by Type III cells) in taste buds altered taste suppression: increasing serotonin with 5-hydroxytryptophan enhanced acid-induced suppression whereas depleting serotonin with para-chlorophenylalanine weakened it.

Sources indicate that finally, population analyses, including UMAP dimensionality reduction, indicate that taste suppression is not limited to a particular subset of gustatory sensory neurons. The findings are consistent with serotonin-dependent paracrine inhibition within taste buds as a contributor to sour-driven suppression in taste mixtures and reveal a compression of gustatory information into hedonic categories as early as at the level of primary sensory neurons.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Swapping just three drinks a week was linked to less weight gain over four years. What mattered was which drinks people gave up.

Recent findings suggest that swapping just three drinks a week was linked to less weight gain over four years. What mattered was which drinks people gave up.

Swapping sugary drinks for water is linked to less weight gain over time, according to a study of more than 140,000 adults.

Replacing them with diet drinks indicates much the same pattern.

Switching from diet drinks to water was linked to a much smaller difference in weight.

Both swaps could make a difference by cutting the calories people get from their usual soft drinks.

A diet version can also preserve the familiar sweet taste, which may make the change easier for some people to stick with.

The findings suggest that the drink someone gives up may matter more for their weight than which of these two alternatives they choose.

The researchers drew on three long-running US studies that followed nurses and other health professionals for a typical period of 28 years.

Participants regularly reported what they drank and how much they weighed, allowing researchers to see how their drinking habits and weight shifted over four-year periods.

The researchers estimated about 1.4 kg less weight gain over four years when three sugary drinks a week were replaced with either water or diet drinks.

The estimated difference for replacing three diet drinks a week with water was only about a tenth of a kilogram over the same period.

People who cut back on sugary drinks tended to gain less weight whether or not they increased their intake of diet drinks.

The researchers estimated the swaps from changes in people’s reported habits, so the study can show associations but cannot establish how much weight any individual would gain or lose after making the switch.

Replacing a regular soft drink with its diet version changes the calories while keeping much of the experience of having a sweet drink.

Switching to water also removes the sweet taste, which may change how much sweetness people prefer over time.

In a separate year-long randomised trial, people assigned to replace sugary drinks with unsweetened ones showed a greater drop in their preferred level of sweetness than those assigned to artificially sweetened drinks (Ebbeling et al., 2020).

That change in taste preference offers a possible reason why an unsweetened choice might become more appealing with time.

The study was published in the American Journal of Clinical Nutrition (Espinosa et al., 2026).

#10533. Breaking: Brain Computes Motion Direction Independently From the Eye

Breaking: Brain Computes Motion Direction Independently From the Eye

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1118 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Neurosciencenews

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that researchers have developed a high-throughput brain-mapping tool that reveals the brain does not simply rely on pre-calculated motion signals from the eye, but also computes the direction of movement independently.
  • Whether ducking a fast-moving ball, stepping back from an oncoming vehicle, or evading an approaching predator, survival depends on the brain’s ability to determine not just that an object is moving, but its exact trajectory in real time.
  • For decades, visual neuroscientists knew that specialized neurons in the mammalian retina fire selectively when stimuli move in specific directions, left, right, up, down, or diagonally.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that researchers have developed a high-throughput brain-mapping tool that reveals the brain does not simply rely on pre-calculated motion signals from the eye, but also computes the direction of movement independently. The study mapped nearly 46,000 mouse brain cells to uncover a dual visual system in the superior colliculus, separating localized object tracking from global self-motion sensing.

Source: UC San Francisco / Nature.

Whether ducking a fast-moving ball, stepping back from an oncoming vehicle, or evading an approaching predator, survival depends on the brain’s ability to determine not just that an object is moving, but its exact trajectory in real time.

For decades, visual neuroscientists knew that specialized neurons in the mammalian retina fire selectively when stimuli move in specific directions, left, right, up, down, or diagonally.

Industry observers note that because these retinal ganglion cells already encode directional vectors, researchers widely assumed the brain simply inherited that pre-calculated motion data passively from the eye. However, no mapping technology existed that could simultaneously trace exact synaptic connections from the retina while identifying the molecular identity of every receiving brain cell.

Now, in a study published in Nature, researchers at UC San Francisco (UCSF) have bridged that technological gap.

Led by co-senior authors Dr. Xin Duan, professor of ophthalmology, and Dr. Evan Feinberg, professor of anatomy, alongside postdoctoral fellow Dr. Fei Wang, the team built a scalable eye-to-brain wiring atlas revealing that specialized circuits in the midbrain compute motion direction completely on their own.

Over the past decade, Duan’s laboratory pioneered anterograde trans-neuronal tracing, a technique in which a fluorescent molecular tracer delivered to the eye crosses synaptic junctions to illuminate only those downstream brain neurons directly receiving retinal input.

To scale this tool from single-circuit tracing into a comprehensive atlas, Wang paired the trans-neuronal tracer with MERFISH (multiplexed error-robust fluorescence in situ hybridization), a spatial transcriptomic method that reads gene activity across thousands of individual cells in a tissue slice simultaneously to pinpoint each neuron’s exact genetic identity.

Applying this combined platform across nearly 46,000 cells in the mouse visual system, the investigators uncovered hundreds of distinct retinal-to-brain connection pairs.

“It’s like an entire atlas we’ve built,” Wang noted. “We’ve uncovered hundreds of pairs of connections between the eye and the brain. We ended up focusing on only one page of this atlas, but there are many left to study in the future.”.

Focusing on the superior colliculus, an evolutionarily conserved midbrain hub essential for visual orientation and rapid motor reflexes, Wang, Feinberg, and Duan recorded real-time neural firing while showing mice high-contrast black bars scrolling across a screen in eight distinct directions.

Combining functional recordings with their molecular wiring map exposed two separate motion-processing architectures operating side by side:.

“We think these sets of cells are doing slightly different things from each other,” Wang explained. “The eye cells detecting direction may specialize in small, local motions like prey or food. The brain cells computing direction sense a larger background movement.”.

The investigators hypothesize that this global background motion signal informs an organism of its own self-motion and spatial trajectory as it navigates through the environment.

Recent findings suggest that beyond resolving a foundational question in visual neuroscience, the high-resolution wiring atlas carries direct translational implications for regenerative medicine and neuroengineering. As researchers advance toward optic nerve regeneration, whole-eye transplantation, and high-resolution visual brain-machine interfaces for patients with glaucoma, trauma, or multiple sclerosis, restoring functional sight requires reconnecting damaged axons to their exact functional targets.

In a recent development, “This is a fundamental mechanism that has been understudied from a basic science perspective, but it also has applied value,” remarked Duan. “If we ever want to repair or restore vision in people, we need to know which neural connections need to be rewired for functional vision.”.

“In addition to providing a blueprint for revealing structural maps of the brain, our study illustrates how the resulting maps can be used to answer longstanding questions regarding brain function,” added Feinberg.

The team notes that their scalable tracer-plus-MERFISH platform can be adapted to map how the eye regulates circadian rhythms, and generalized to chart cell-to-cell connectivity across any organ system in the body.

Does the eye do all the work of detecting which way things move?

Recent findings suggest that no. While specialized cells in the retina detect motion direction and send that data to the brain, UCSF researchers discovered a second group of neurons in the brain’s superior colliculus that independently calculates motion direction using basic visual inputs, even when the eye’s own direction-sensing cells are turned off.

Why does the brain have two different systems for sensing motion?

Researchers believe the two pathways handle different visual jobs: the eye’s direction-sensing cells appear specialized for tracking small, local moving targets (like food, prey, or a flying ball), while the brain’s independent motion-computing cells detect large-scale background movement to help track how your own body is moving through space.

How could this brain-mapping tool help restore vision in the future?

Recent findings suggest that to successfully develop eye transplants, optic nerve repairs, or visual brain-machine interfaces for conditions like glaucoma or multiple sclerosis, scientists need an exact wiring diagram showing which eye cells connect to which functional brain circuits. This new atlas provides that precise rewiring blueprint.

TransA-MERFISH reveals divergent post-retinal direction-selective circuits.

A major goal in neuroscience is to map the transformation of information as it flows through the brain. For example, neurons at many levels of the visual hierarchy are attuned to motion direction. However, links between motion-selective computations and cell types at various stages of the visual hierarchy remain unidentified. A key first step in delineating these relationships is to map the wiring diagrams that connect different motion-selective cell types.

Here we establish a systematic, cell-type-specific circuit-mapping method, combining an anterograde trans-neuronal fluorescent tracer (mWGA–mCherry) with spatial transcriptomics (multiplexed error-robust fluorescence in situ hybridization (MERFISH)) to establish TransA-MERFISH. We used TransA-MERFISH to comprehensively map the synaptic target cell types of four retinal ganglion cell subclasses in superior colliculus (SC) at cell-type resolution.

These experiments unexpectedly revealed that retinal on–off direction-selective ganglion cells (ooDSGCs) innervate several direction-selective SC cell types, but do not innervate a SC cell type that was previously reported to display strong direction-selective responses.

Industry observers note that we validated these results using orthogonal approaches and demonstrated the sensitivity and specificity of TransA-MERFISH. Functional studies of SC activity before and after ablation of retinal direction-selective circuits confirmed that these computationally distinct, ooDSGC-dependent and -independent direction-selective cell types are commingled in SC.

Together, our study establishes TransA-MERFISH as a robust framework for mapping wiring diagrams at the cell-type level and uncovers divergent computational mechanisms of motion detection in early visual processing.

#10532. Breaking: How to Deal With the Grief of an Aging Body

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1009 w)

Breaking: How to Deal With the Grief of an Aging Body

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1009 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Berkeley

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Body changes can raise disturbing feelings, such as looking in a mirror and seeing a reflection that may feel spiritually empty, unproductive, ugly, or weak.
  • Unpleasant sensations such as pain, pins and needles, soreness coursing through limbs, and an inexplicable fog filling the head are a reminder that this body is not the same you anymore, prompting us to wish there was a way to get back there.
  • This is the disillusionment that most of the population will face at some point in life, through aging, chronic pain, or invisible illness (a disease or health problem that cannot be externally seen, including autoimmune diseases, chronic pain and fatigue, and recently, long COVID).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Body changes can raise disturbing feelings, such as looking in a mirror and seeing a reflection that may feel spiritually empty, unproductive, ugly, or weak.

Unpleasant sensations such as pain, pins and needles, soreness coursing through limbs, and an inexplicable fog filling the head are a reminder that this body is not the same you anymore, prompting us to wish there was a way to get back there. It may feel impossible to live well unless you do.

This is the disillusionment that most of the population will face at some point in life, through aging, chronic pain, or invisible illness (a disease or health problem that cannot be externally seen, including autoimmune diseases, chronic pain and fatigue, and recently, long COVID).

Industry observers note that recent global estimates suggest one in five people are currently experiencing chronic pain. The most prevalent chronic pain reported by adults ages 75 and over includes low back pain and migraine, while tension-type headaches are more often experienced by younger adults. Chronic illness (diabetes, heart disease, and other mid-to-late-life diagnoses) affects about three-quarters of the world population.

Despite how common chronic illness is worldwide, the nuances of navigating a changing body are not often discussed. It’s time for an honest, evidence-based conversation about what it means to navigate chronic pain and illness, aging and transforming identity post-diagnosis, and how to grieve this loss and maintain meaning through these changes.

Research suggest that those with internalized stigma of chronic illness are more preoccupied with how their illness detracts from their view of themselves, and also have a greater tendency to overlook positive aspects of life with a chronic illness.

According to recent reports, psychologists have observed how preoccupation with illness or pain is often accompanied by other grief behaviors. A 2025 study explored how Danish chronic illness patients navigated loss and growth. The study found that many with chronic illness find themselves mourning the life that they thought they would have, often leading to loss of motivation and joy in everyday life.

The perception of losing the life they had once envisioned is often accompanied by a focus on getting back to the “before illness” version of themselves as people struggle to accept how their body has changed, perhaps in how it looks but definitely in how it feels.

These changes and associated feelings of loss often permeate a person’s sense of identity, as well as their perceived roles within social relationships. Many report a fear of burdening others, especially loved ones, often describing feelings of guilt that “others have it worse than I do.” This is where internalized stigma festers.

Sources indicate that some people have also described feelings of anger, isolation, shame, and exhaustion accompanying sadness. Meanwhile, others have expressed frustration over a gradual loss rather than a “clean break,” accompanied by the inability to find closure.

Sources indicate that first, it’s important to understand why accepting this continuous loss feels so impossible. Theories of control in psychology state that humans desire control or the ability to achieve a desired outcome according to our own standards.

The best and most enduring of our articles, podcasts, and videos about getting older.

When that ability is seen as stripped away, people are more likely to experience negative mental health symptoms, like anxiety, depression, and even grief. Specifically, feelings of diminished perceived control (subjective belief about our ability to achieve desired outcomes) occur when we face continuous roadblocks to living our desired life because of chronic illness.

It has been revealed that one of the major consequences of loss and major life change is that it can disrupt meaning and challenge identity, purpose, and assumptions about the future. At a time when people feel there is little they can control, psychologist Robert Neimeyer’s Meaning Reconstruction Theory poses the questions: “How do I move forward?” and “What matters most?”.

Industry observers note that while the original theory was proposed as an approach to coping with the loss of a loved one, the process is somewhat similar to grieving the close ally that is your body. This theory approaches grief by making sense of the loss and finding ways to rebuild a sense of purpose in a changed life (and body).

To answer relevant questions about how to move forward with chronic illness, two ongoing approaches are needed: integrating the loss and recentering purpose and meaning.

Integrating the loss may look like processing significant bodily losses in therapy, finding trusted loved ones to talk about the loss with, and focusing on being realistic about your current body without judgment.

Second, recentering purpose during this major life change involves understanding your why: why is this loss so significant to you, why does it hurt? Maybe it’s because you love hiking in the mountains and a new diagnosis with arthritis feels like the end of this joy. Part of rebuilding meaning is finding new approaches to fulfilling this purpose—perhaps hiking may look different, but nature can be accessed and loved with chronic illness present.

It has been revealed that rebuilding meaning might also look like making meaning from this loss: What has this change taught you about yourself, about the impact you can make? Approaching present and future with this perspective helps process grief in a more protective way.

Living with chronic pain, illness, and the changes that come with aging often involves grieving physical loss, but also shifts in purpose, relationships, identity, and future aims. While these changes challenge our perceived control and purpose, the Meaning Reconstruction Theory suggests that acceptance and growth comes with integrating loss and rebuilding purpose alongside these changes.

Although the present is different than anticipated, fulfillment is still possible with your current body.

Li-elle Rapaport is a doctoral candidate in clinical psychology and a supervised therapist. Her clinical work is informed by evidence-based approaches, including Acceptance and Commitment Therapy (ACT) and Mindful Self-Compassion, and her doctoral research focuses on aging and mental health.

Industry News: Ultraprocessed Foods Alter Food-Reward Brain Activity

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Ultraprocessed foods, products formulated with industrial processing methods and ingredients rarely found in a home kitchen, account for more than half of the calories consumed by young adults in the United States.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, A controlled feeding trial reveals that just two weeks on a diet high in ultraprocessed foods alters brain reward responses in emerging adults ages 18 to 21, while leaving adults ages 22 to 25 unaffected. The fMRI study highlights blunted activation in the developing orbitofrontal cortex, a key region for food valuation and self-control, even when diets are strictly matched for calories, sugar, fat, and nutrients.

Source: Virginia Tech / Obesity.

Ultraprocessed foods, products formulated with industrial processing methods and ingredients rarely found in a home kitchen, account for more than half of the calories consumed by young adults in the United States. While extensive research links these foods to obesity, metabolic syndrome, and cardiovascular disease, neuroscientists are increasingly uncovering how industrial processing directly interacts with the developing human brain.

In a controlled feeding study published this month in the journal Obesity, researchers at Virginia Tech’s Fralin Biomedical Research Institute at VTC and Department of Human Nutrition, Foods, and Exercise found that emerging adults ages 18 to 21 exhibit distinct neural changes in food-reward circuitry after consuming an ultraprocessed diet for just two weeks.

Industry observers note that led by first author Dr. Emma Leslie alongside neuroscientist Dr. Alex DiFeliceantonio and registered dietitian Dr. Brenda Davy, the findings complement earlier results from the same trial showing that 18- to 21-year-olds consumed excess calories at a buffet meal after eating ultraprocessed foods, even when they were no longer hungry.

It has been revealed that to separate the effects of industrial food processing from basic nutritional content, the researchers recruited 22 healthy adults ages 18 to 25 (including seven participants ages 21 or younger) for a randomized crossover feeding trial. Each participant followed two strictly controlled diets for two weeks apiece, separated by a four-week washout period:.

Critically, both diets were engineered to have identical macronutrient profiles (50% carbohydrates, 35% fat, 15% protein), matching levels of fiber, added sugars, saturated fat, sodium, energy density, and overall nutritional quality, calibrated to keep each participant’s body weight stable.

Before and after each two-week dietary phase, participants underwent functional MRI (fMRI) brain scans while receiving small sips of an ultraprocessed milkshake or a tasteless control solution through a specialized delivery tube.

When the researchers analyzed the neuroimaging data, they discovered a striking developmental divide:.

“Among the younger participants, consuming a diet high in ultraprocessed foods for just two weeks was associated with decreased brain response to a rewarding food — a milkshake — in the orbitofrontal cortex,” explained Leslie, who conducted the work as a doctoral student at Virginia Tech and is now a postdoctoral associate at the University of Michigan.

Located just behind the eyes, the orbitofrontal cortex is one of the final regions of the human brain to finish maturing, continuing to remodel into the mid- to late 20s. It plays a central role in evaluating food rewards, regulating cravings, and exerting executive self-control to stop eating.

Because the two diets were matched across nutritional metrics, the findings point toward non-nutritive properties of ultraprocessed foods, such as chemical additives, emulsifiers, texture alterations, or compounds generated during industrial processing, as potential drivers of altered brain signaling.

“This study is vital because you have this change in an area of the brain known to govern self-control and potentially put a stop to eating,” said DiFeliceantonio, associate professor at the Fralin Biomedical Research Institute and interim co-director of its Center for Health Behaviors Research. “This is giving us insight into how ultraprocessed foods are affecting the bodies and brains of younger people, who might be especially vulnerable to their effects. And that’s important to know for things like dietary guidelines, doctor recommendations, and policy decisions.”.

While the researchers note that the sample size was small and the age-based findings were exploratory, and did not directly correlate individual fMRI shifts with buffet calorie intake, the results highlight adolescence and early adulthood as critical windows of neurodevelopmental sensitivity.

In a recent development, next, DiFeliceantonio and Davy blueprint to investigate whether adolescents under 18, who consume the highest proportion of ultraprocessed foods of any U.S. demographic, show even stronger neural sensitivity, and whether brain responses recover once individuals return to whole-food diets.

How do ultraprocessed foods affect the brains of young adults?

A Virginia Tech study found that after eating a diet high in ultraprocessed foods for just two weeks, young adults ages 18 to 21 showed decreased brain activity in the orbitofrontal cortex, a region involved in food reward, valuation, and self-control, when tasting a milkshake. Adults ages 22 to 25 did not show these brain changes.

Was the brain effect simply caused by extra sugar, fat, or calories?

Recent findings suggest that no. Both the ultraprocessed diet and the unprocessed comparison diet contained the exact same amounts of calories, carbohydrates, fat, protein, added sugars, saturated fat, fiber, and sodium. This suggests that industrial food processing or additives themselves, rather than basic nutrients, drove the brain changes.

Why are 18- to 21-year-olds more sensitive to ultraprocessed foods than slightly older adults?

In a recent development, the orbitofrontal cortex is one of the last brain regions to finish developing, continuing to mature into the mid- to late 20s. Because this self-control and reward-evaluation circuit is still actively wiring in 18- to 21-year-olds, it appears more sensitive to dietary shifts.

We investigated if a high-UPF diet alters brain response to milkshake compared with a diet free from UPF in emerging adults, who are in a critical brain development period and typically consume high amounts of UPF.

Industry observers note that in a randomized controlled crossover trial participants aged 18–25 years completed two 2-week controlled feeding periods including a UPF (81% UPF) and non-UPF (0% UPF) diet. Before and after each diet intervention, participants consumed milkshake concomitant with functional magnetic resonance imaging.

According to recent reports, in the entire cohort, there were no differences between diet conditions in brain response. An exploratory analysis revealed orbitofrontal cortex response to milkshake decreased after the UPF diet and increased following the non-UPF diet in late adolescents (18–21 years) but not young adults (22–25 years). In all participants, habitual UPF intake (g) was positively associated with orbitofrontal cortex response to milkshake, independent of diet condition.

An acute UPF dietary intervention may only alter brain response in late adolescents. Further work is needed to determine potential vulnerability of late adolescents to changes in dietary UPF on brain response to rewards.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Art Basel will compensate dealers for the early closure of its Paris fair, held from 20-23 October in the Grand Palais, the fair tech giant announced today (11th November), on a French national holiday.

The fair was forced to shut down its Parisian outing two days early because of violent rioting in the French capital. Since then, dealers have been demanding compensation for their lost sales and stand fees. Indeed, soon after the closure the French Comité Professionnel des Galeries d’Art (CPGA) sent a strongly worded letter to the fair director, Karim Crippa. It accused the firm of not consulting with dealers—the CPGA represents 57 of the fair’s 211 exhibitors—and of showing “disrespect, even contempt” for them.

Recent findings suggest that the closure hit the smaller dealers particularly hard, since the biggest galleries tended to make sales on the opening days, whereas the smaller dealers, mainly sited on the upper floor of the Grand Palais, depended on the two weekend days for business. The letter said it expected “concrete proposals” for this compensation.

According to recent reports, crippa has responded to the letter with an offer of a reduction across the board of 20% of stand fees to all participants. He remarked: “We believe this approach offers a fair and considered way forward, reflecting our appreciation of the partnership we share and our commitment to strengthening it further.”.

Philippe Charpentier of Mor Charpentier gallery, who is the president of the CPGA, tells The Art Newspaper that the compensation rate is what the committee expected.

Recent findings suggest that nonetheless, if one calculates in percentages, the fair was open for three-and-a-half days—its ultra-VIP Avant-Première timeslot began at 3pm on Tuesday 20 October, and the fair closed on Friday—instead of the projected five-and-a-half. The fair was therefore shortened by about 36%.

Speaking about the decision to close the fair early, Noah Horowitz, the chief executive of Art Basel, tells The Art Newspaper: “We stand by the decision to close. We feel it was in the right interest of all the parties involved. It was a very difficult decision, but we stand by it.”.

Recent findings suggest that asked about the decision to close for the two days—when unrest was only expected on the Saturday—he claims: “Given the uncertainty surrounding the impact and the duration of the planned demonstrations and access to the Grand Palais, we simply couldn't be confident that conditions would allow us to reopen safely on Sunday. An event of this size and scale is incredibly complex, and some exhibitors had also expressed serious concerns about leaving artworks unattended in the Grand Palais on the weekend. We concluded that closing the fair early was in the best interests of the art, the staff and ultimately the visitors.”.

Recent findings suggest that horowitz is not prepared to comment on other aspects of the closure—for example, questions of insurance or the firm’s relationship with the Grand Palais, for which MCH paid €10.6m to rent the space for seven years in 2022. Horowitz claims that MCH, the parent company of the Basel group of art fairs, is "fully committed to delivering the 2027 edition of the fair".
